title: Prototype Focus-Group Report and Evidence Audit
paragraphs:
Appendix G
Prototype Focus-Group Report and Evi-
dence Audit
This appendix incorporates the merged FGD report. Its narrative-level nd-
ings inform Sections 6.7 and 5.9; the underlying participant records remain unver-
ied; a 160-segment machine transcript is included, but speaker attribution and
human verication are pending.
G.1
Purpose and Evidentiary Scope
This report integrates two narrative accounts of a focus-group discussion (FGD) in-
volving university students and a walkthrough of LOKLOK, a proposed social media
radio application. Its purpose is to clarify the audience needs and design questions
suggested by those accounts: the relationship between listening and creating, the
appeal and constraints of collaborative broadcasting, expectations around institu-
tional access, and the usability of a wireframe interface. It does not establish the
platform's originality, market success, or eects on student behaviour.
The material comprises the earlier narrative (Account A) and the expanded
narrative supplied as FGD2.tex (Account B), together with their PDFs. Account A
is retained in the source archive, while this document is the merged report. The two
268

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
269
narratives repeat the same four domains, lexical counts, and frame references. They
are therefore treated as overlapping accounts of one reported session, not two focus
groups, independent corroboration, or separate participant samples. A 160-segment
machine transcript of the session audio is included.
The audiovisual recordings,
speaker attribution, and participant roster remain unavailable; the transcript is
used for semantic embedding, not for audited quotation. A subsequently supplied
le, fgd_analysis_parts.json, contains seven model-generated summaries. It is
designated Supplement C, not another focus group or an independent corroborating
source. The proposed revised LaTeX accompanying that export is treated as a set of
candidate claims to review, not as evidence that the primary materials have been re-
covered. Section G.4 records the adjudication. Throughout, reported account means
a statement present in either supplied narrative; interpretation means an analytical
reading of that account; and verication requirement identies the evidence needed
to assess it. None of these labels turns a paraphrase into a participant quotation.
Focus groups derive their distinctive value from interaction among partici-
pants, including exchanges, disagreements, and responses to one another, rather than
simply collecting several individual opinions at once (Kitzinger, 1995). In this case,
the distinction between a moderator-led product demonstration and participant-led
discussion is especially important. Both accounts report extensive moderator ex-
planation, but the balance of contributions cannot be established without speaker-
labelled records.
Statements explaining how LOKLOK is intended to work are
therefore not treated as evidence that participants endorsed those features.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
270
G.2
Study Context and Reporting Completeness
Both accounts describe a university conference-room session conducted in colloquial
Egyptian Arabic, an English translation, and smartphone interaction with applica-
tion wireframes. Account B explicitly situates the proposed campus restriction in
the Ahram Canadian University (ACU) context. This claries the reported insti-
tutional setting without establishing each participant's aliation, the exact venue,
recruitment procedure, or ethics review.
Account A gives an approximate duration of 28 minutes; Account B reports
1,675.33 seconds (27 minutes 55.33 seconds). These descriptions are compatible as
rounded and more precise reported durations. The latter is not newly measured
metadata, however, and it does not resolve the visual reference at 30 minutes 30
seconds. Section G.9 reconciles the arithmetic and records the remaining source dis-
crepancy. Additional recording details from Account B are retained in Section G.8.
Table G.1 identies the principal information needed for a source-based re-
port. COREQ oers reporting prompts for interviews and focus groups, while APA's
qualitative reporting standards emphasise the transparent presentation of research
design, researcher involvement, analysis, and evidence (Levitt et al., 2018; Tong et
al., 2007). These sources guide the audit; citing them does not establish checklist
compliance, ethical approval, or study quality.

No survey sample size elsewhere in the thesis is assigned to this FGD. Nor can
sampling adequacy or saturation be asserted from the length of the account. The
information-power approach relates qualitative sample adequacy to the study aim,
sample specicity, theoretical framing, dialogue, and analysis strategy rather than
to a universal numerical threshold (Malterud et al., 2016). Developed for individual

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
272
interview studies, that approach does not prescribe the number or composition of
focus groups. Those considerations cannot yet be assessed here.
G.3
Analytical Approach and Source Verication
G.3.1
A Provisional, Framework-Informed Reading
The revision retains the four shared domains as provisional organising categories and
integrates Account B's proposed links to the thesis framework. The domains were
not newly generated through inductive coding of a transcript. Thematic analysis
involves interpreting patterned meaning, and its theoretical and procedural choices
should be explicit (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Here, the immediate aim is narrower: to
distinguish reported experiences, moderator explanations, analytical interpretations,
and proposed design responses without overstating their evidentiary status.
If primary records become available, a framework-informed analysis would
be a suitable option to consider. A matrix can link cases or interaction episodes to
categories while retaining contextual summaries and source references (Gale et al.,
2013). The present codebook is a starting point for that work, not proof that it has
been performed. New categories, contradictory cases, and revisions to the initial four
domains must remain possible. The researcher should identify the chosen analytical
tradition rather than combine incompatible quality criteria: intercoder agreement is
not a universal requirement of reexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2021).
No agreement statistic or independent coding is claimed here.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
273
G.3.2
Language, Translation, and Quotations
Translation is an interpretive part of qualitative research, not a neutral replacement
of words. Decisions about idiom and expression can alter meaning (van Nes et al.,
2010). For this study, a proposed verication record should retain the Egyptian
Arabic extract alongside the English translation, with a speaker code, source times-
tamp, and a note explaining consequential translation choices. A bilingual review
should be documented if undertaken, not assumed. Ambiguity, disagreement, or
hesitation should not be removed merely to produce more uent academic prose.
Because no primary transcript or recording was supplied, this report provides
no purported verbatim participant quotations. Supplement C contains text labelled
as original Arabic and translations, but those labels do not establish transcription
delity or speaker identity. The underlying strings are retained in the controlled re-
view record, not promoted into participant testimony. Expressions used as interface
names or analytical labels, such as Boost and Podcast Paradox, are not presented as
quotations from identied participants. Before an extract is published as evidence,
its wording, translation, attribution, and permitted use must be checked against the
original record. An unintelligible segment should remain marked as uncertain rather
than reconstructed from expectations.
G.3.3
Proposed Verication Sequence
The following sequence is a prospective procedure for this material, not a retrospec-
tive account of completed analysis:
1. Establish a le inventory and preserve the original recording, transcript, pro-

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
274
totype version, and permissions records. Assign stable le identiers and doc-
ument any edited or translated derivatives.
2. Reconcile the recording duration and timestamp origin. Link each extract and
observation to the same source version; document osets where necessary.
3. Identify participant and moderator turns using pseudonymous codes. Retain
the surrounding exchange so that prompted agreement is distinguishable from
an independently introduced concern.
4. Review the Arabic and English records together. Record uncertain speech,
translation choices, overlapping speech, and observable actions separately.
5. Apply and revise the provisional codebook. Maintain source-linked analytical
memos, including divergent experiences and explanations that do not support
the anticipated design benet.
6. Reassess every thematic claim and any descriptive count against those records.
Report only the procedures actually completed and retain an audit trail of
changes.
G.4
Review of the Supplemental Analysis Export
Supplement C is a JSON array of seven text strings, each containing generated
questions, proposed answers, themes, or quality cautions.
It contains neither a
structured primary transcript with attributable turns nor a collection of 20 visual
frames. No recording, frame images, source-to-output alignment, prompt, execution

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
275
log, or independently reviewed translation accompanies it. The researcher identi-
es the export as output from an instruction-tuned 7B model; the le itself does
not establish the exact model version, quantisation, input coverage, or generation
settings.
The admissible contribution is an additional set of review leads and a record
of limitations in the generated analysis. It does not change the primary-evidence
status reported in Section G.1. References to unveried speakers occur in the output,
but no inspected transcript supports the stronger claim that every original segment
carries that label. Nor may an unattributed sentence be reassigned to the moderator
or the group merely because that role seems plausible.
G.4.1
Internal Consistency and Translation Checks
Part numbers below are one-based positions in the supplied JSON array, not par-
ticipant identiers or independently timed recording segments. In Part 2, an Arabic
expression referring to a room is paired with an English rendering that locates the
microphone in a car.
Part 1 renders a colloquial vehicle-listening expression as
listening in the Arabic language. These are translation inconsistencies within the
export; identifying them does not verify that either extract was actually spoken.
Named-person renderings also require checking against the recording rather than
being accepted from the English gloss alone. Translation choices should preserve
source meaning and uncertainty rather than create a more uent but altered ac-
count (van Nes et al., 2010).
Some purported extracts contain Chinese or Cyrillic material mixed with
Arabic, while several timestamps are incomplete, malformed, or placeholders. Part 5

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT

apparently unnished text. These observations warrant review of the original inputs
and generation logs; they do not establish why the artefacts occurred. No missing
words, speakers, or time boundaries are reconstructed to make the export appear
complete.

277
G.4.2
What Changes in the Interpretation
The four provisional domains remain in place.
Supplement C suggests checking
whether preferred programme length varies and whether registration instructions or
error feedback are understood. These are follow-up questions within FGD-T1 and
FGD-T4, not newly established participant experiences. Its account of unrestricted
access also conicts with the campus-only descriptions in Accounts A and B; this is
retained as an unresolved discrepancy, not evidence that the participants debated
or agreed on an open-access policy.
Repeated vocalisation-like strings in Parts 57 are treated as unresolved tran-
script artefacts. They are not coded as silence, non-participation, hesitation, a tech-
nical failure, or active wireframe use without checking the recording and aligned
visual evidence. Sparse or uninterpretable output cannot establish that no substan-
tive speech occurred. Likewise, generated statements that everyone agreed do not
establish consensus when the original interaction and speakers are unavailable.
The proposed bilingual quotations are consequently not inserted as empirical
extracts. A review record retains the candidate wording, its JSON part locator, the
disputed rendering, and the decision needed before use. No synthetic quote becomes
a participant record, calibration weight, factual answer key, or prompt instruction
to reproduce a favourable outcome. The export may inform quality checks and later
source review, but does not independently conrm the existing themes or validate
either proposed simulation engine.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
278
G.5
Provisional Thematic Interpretation
The four domains below synthesise the two supplied narratives, not newly veried
transcripts. Supplement C has been reviewed for candidate additions but is not
treated as independent corroboration. Each separates the reported account from
its possible meaning and the limits of that interpretation. External methodological
citations explain how the material is handled; they do not authenticate the local
observations.
G.5.1
FGD-T1: Contextual Listening and Selective Publication
Reported account. Both accounts describe listening during travel and at home,
interest in radio storytelling, and a reference to older radio serials. They also recount
an individual who owns a microphone and records privately but does not publish
those recordings. Account B explicitly attributes this practice to self-training and
preparation and says that recordings are discarded. This reported explanation is
retained, but speaker identity, verbatim wording, and interactional context remain
unveried in the machine transcript.
Interpretation. The account suggests a useful distinction between listening,
practising, and publishing. Possessing recording equipment or enjoying audio does
not necessarily imply a wish to broadcast publicly. The draft calls this tension the
Podcast Paradox; here, that expression is retained only as a provisional analytical
label, not a validated construct or a demonstrated characteristic of the wider student
population.
Alternative readings and implications. Unpublished recordings could

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
279
reect deliberate private practice, privacy preferences, limited time, self-imposed
production standards, or a lack of interest in an audience. The reported self-training
explanation deserves priority over an imposed anxiety interpretation, although its
meaning and context still require source checking. Other explanations should be
explored, not attributed to that individual without evidence. A defensible design
question is therefore whether students want dierent routes from listening to private
practice, collaborative creation, and public sharing. Non-public participation should
not automatically be framed as failure or a decit.
G.5.2
FGD-T2: Collaborative Broadcasting and Choice
Reported account. The moderator reportedly described a broadcasting mechanic
requiring a peer invitation or co-host. The narrative characterises the reaction as
favourable, but provides no attributable extracts, contrary responses, or evidence of
subsequent use. Account B also develops an analogy with traditional radio call-ins:
inviting a peer to co-host is presented as a way to make the broadcast a shared
conversation. This is the account's design rationale, not evidence that a caller's role
and a co-host's role are equivalent. The rule is treated as part of the walkthrough
description, not as a veried feature of a deployed application.
Interpretation. Co-hosting is a candidate means of making an audio ex-
change feel conversational rather than like an individual performance. This is a
plausible reading of the accounts, not a measured reduction in anxiety, eort, or
cognitive demand. Source-based analysis should ask who introduced this idea and
how others responded, preserving the interaction rather than counting armative
words alone (Kitzinger, 1995).

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
280
Alternative readings and implications.
Mandatory co-hosting might
also restrict participation when a peer is unavailable, when a student prefers in-
dependent expression, or when social exposure is unwelcome.
These are design
questions proposed in this review, not diculties demonstrated in the session. Op-
tional co-hosting, private rehearsal, and alternative contribution routes should be
compared with the mandatory model before claiming that one arrangement lowers
barriers for everyone.
G.5.3
FGD-T3: Institutional Eligibility, Trust, and Privacy
Reported account. Both accounts describe a university-ID and PIN entry process,
explained through an ATM analogy, and a platform initially limited to university stu-
dents, with Account B naming the ACU context. The narratives attribute benets
involving trust and community to this arrangement, but do not supply participant-
level evidence of those judgements or an assessment of the authentication system.
Interpretation. Institutional eligibility, perceived trust, condentiality, and
technical security are separate questions. The described entry rule alone establishes
none of the latter three. In particular, restricting membership does not demonstrate
the absence of harassment, prove the validity of research responses, or show that
students feel comfortable speaking under an institutional identity.
Alternative readings and implications. A bounded community could
be welcoming for some students and expose others to unwanted visibility.
The
next evaluation should ask what identity information is displayed, who can access
recordings, how complaints are handled, and whether eligible students can obtain
or recover access. Preferences for named and pseudonymous participation should

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
281
be explored rather than presumed. These are proposed evaluation topics; neither
preference nor a security outcome was measured in the material available here.
G.5.4
FGD-T4: Interface Cues, Invitations, and Idle Content
Reported account. The narrative describes proles, avatars, names, timestamps,
a text-based Boost invitation, and music or advertising when no broadcast is ac-
tive. It also reports smartphone interaction during the walkthrough. The available
documents do not establish which functions were interactive, which were static rep-
resentations, or which were explained only by the moderator.
Interpretation. These descriptions identify candidate interface functions:
communicating who is present, inviting an audience, and explaining what happens
when no conversation is available. They do not demonstrate successful navigation,
low cognitive load, sustained engagement, or an intuitive interface. Such conclusions
would require task-linked evidence and the participants' own accounts, not merely
a statement that screens were tapped or swiped.
Alternative readings and implications. Future evaluation should con-
sider whether invitations are understandable, whether idle-state content is clearly
identied, and whether users can control unwanted playback. Relevant accessibil-
ity checks can draw on WCAG 2.2, including applicable text alternatives, contrast,
navigation, and media-control criteria (World Wide Web Consortium, 2024). This
is a proposal for evaluation, not a nding of accessibility or a claim of conformance
by the prototype. Applicable criteria must be selected for the actual interface and
media format.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
282
G.6
Working Codebook and Relationships

Codes should be assigned to source-linked segments, not to entire people. A segment
may have more than one relevant code; a moderator's feature description must re-

are proposed coding conventions for this report, not a completed coding result.

G.6.1
Relationship to Epistemic Systems Theory
Account B links the domains to Epistemic Systems Theory (EST), the framework
proposed by the thesis author. This theoretical reading is retained as a sensitising
interpretation: it identies questions to investigate, not propositions conrmed by
the FGD. It follows the narrative synthesis rather than replacing source-based anal-
ysis. A framework matrix can make such interpretive connections traceable while
keeping the original evidence and alternative readings visible (Gale et al., 2013).
In particular, Account B's alignment of institutional exclusivity with EST-P3
needs qualication. In the thesis, EST-P3 concerns the psychometric accountability
of consequential metrics. This FGD account supplies neither a measurement model
nor reliability or validity evidence for such a metric. Institutional access may be
discussed as governance context, but cannot stand in for psychometric validation.
Likewise, no network-diversity or misinformation-diusion observations are supplied

The integrated interpretation is therefore about participation choices within
a proposed design, not demonstrated epistemic gains. Private practice may be an in-
tended activity rather than failed publication; collaboration may be welcome without
being compulsory; and institutional membership may be valued without implying
comfort with identiable speech. These alternatives connect the four domains with-
out forcing all accounts into a single product success narrative. Any later linkage to
survey ndings must distinguish qualitative meanings from numerical associations
and establish the provenance of each dataset before claiming convergence.
G.7
Lexical Counts: Audit and Proposed Reanalysis
Both accounts assign the same frequencies to six grouped English terms, but no
transcript, search dictionary, tokenisation rule, or speaker-specic denominator ac-
companies them. Table G.6 preserves those gures for traceability only. Repetition

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT
285
across the accounts is not replication, and the gures are not added together. They
are not independently reproduced results and are excluded from the sub-
stantive conclusions of this report. The six categories must not be summed
into a corpus size: overlap, eligibility, and unit of counting are unspecied.

transcript contains. They do not establish the relative importance of themes or participant en-

In summative qualitative content analysis, counts are followed by contextual
interpretation; they do not replace it (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005). For this FGD, a term
could appear in a moderator explanation, a participant's objection, or an unrelated
example.
Its repetition alone cannot establish interest, trust, or a psychological
barrier. Counts from an English translation must also be identied as counts of
that translation, not as frequencies in the original Arabic speech.
If lexical analysis is retained, the researcher should rst specify the corpus ver-
sion, eligible speaker turns, treatment of llers, word boundaries, case and inection
handling, category dictionary, and overlapping matches. One proposed descriptive
measure is the frequency per 1,000 eligible words within each speaker role:

G.8

G.10
Reexivity, Ethics, and Inclusive Interpretation
Researcher position and prior commitments can shape both the research encounter
and its interpretation (Berger, 2015). The accounts' product-oriented language and
emphasis on favourable responses warrant particular reexive attention. The mod-
erator's relationship to the students and the product should be documented. En-
thusiasm, politeness, prompted agreement, and substantive endorsement should be
considered as alternative readings, not presumed equivalent. Any institutional power
relationship is a question to investigate, not a fact established by the current les.
The revised report does not treat students as a homogeneous generation or
assume shared levels of condence, digital access, language prociency, or willing-
ness to appear publicly. Future recruitment and facilitation should consider whose

experiences are absent and what participation arrangements people prefer. Listen-
ing without broadcasting, using an alternative mode of expression, or choosing not
to answer must not be interpreted as lesser competence. The supplied narratives
provide no basis for subgroup comparisons or claims that the prototype is inclusive
in practice.
For any further use of the underlying material, the researcher should verify
the applicable ethics review and permissions rather than insert a retrospective claim
of approval. The record should distinguish agreement to participate, recording per-
mission, and any permission for quotation, image publication, or secondary reuse.
Identifying information should be limited to what the approved research purpose
requires, with access and disclosure arrangements documented. A group discussion
also requires attention to what participants may disclose about one another; insti-
tutional membership alone is not a condentiality safeguard. These are proposed
safeguards for this project, not a statement that they were implemented.
Reporting what was actually done, including departures from the intended
procedure and unresolved evidence gaps, is more informative than claiming un-
qualied rigour. Qualitative reporting standards support that transparency while
accommodating dierent research traditions (Levitt et al., 2018).

G.12
Limitations, Transferability, and Conclusion
The decisive limitation is evidentiary: the narratives and supplemental generated
summaries cannot replace a veried human transcript, the recordings, participant
information, and analytical records. The new export increases the material avail-
able for critique, not the amount of veried primary data. Its descriptions cannot
support audited quotation, a veried frequency analysis, or a completed audiovisual
triangulation. Unresolved session timing further constrains reconstruction. The ab-
sence of documented sampling and recruitment prevents assessment of the range of
perspectives included or omitted.
There are also limits to the reported design. A moderator-led wireframe walk-
through does not establish behaviour during ordinary use, and favourable comments
do not demonstrate sustained adoption, reduced anxiety, or improved learning. The
absence of a comparison design and veried outcomes precludes causal conclusions.
Transfer to another study requires an explicit judgement about dierences in partic-
ipants, institutional setting, language, prototype, and research purpose, rather than
treating this account as universally applicable evidence.
Within these boundaries, the merged accounts oer a coherent set of ques-
tions about audio participation: how listening relates to publication, when collabo-
ration is welcome, what institutional membership means to users, and how interface
choices support or obstruct their intentions. The contribution of this revision is to
integrate the reported context and design rationale while making those questions
